Inferior alveolar nerve injury

Small trials report sensory improvement after selected post-extraction and implant-related injuries, while earlier pooled evidence shows little short-term effect.

Summary of the Evidence

PBM may support sensory recovery after selected inferior alveolar nerve injuries, but certainty varies by injury cause and follow-up. A 2023 review found no clear benefit in the first two weeks and favorable pooled results after 30 days. Newer sham-controlled trials report promising results in post-extraction hypoesthesia and implant-related paresthesia.

Human and clinical evidence

The exact database category contains 47 titles: 17 randomized-trial reports, including one retracted publication, 12 other human clinical reports, ten animal publications, and eight reviews or syntheses. The retracted report is excluded from efficacy interpretation. Publication totals are not counts of independent patient cohorts, and reviews overlap primary studies.

Ma et al. included 15 randomized trials in a systematic review and 14 in meta-analysis. Two-point discrimination did not significantly differ within 48 hours or at 14 days. Pooled estimates favored PBM at 30 days (SMD −0.63, 95% CI −0.97 to −0.29) and 60 days (SMD −1.10, 95% CI −1.44 to −0.76). Most included injuries followed orthognathic surgery, with fewer studies after third-molar extraction or fracture (Ma et al. 2023).

A 2026 double-blind sham-controlled trial enrolled 60 adults with hypoesthesia after mandibular third-molar extraction. Direct PBM improved two-point discrimination and monofilament outcomes versus sham. At day 30, the two-point-discrimination change was −2.6 ± 1.7 mm with direct PBM and −0.8 ± 1.1 mm with sham; monofilament sensitivity improved by at least one grade in 80% versus 25%. All groups received mecobalamin, and the findings apply to this selected post-extraction population (Ma et al. 2026).

A separate 24-person randomized trial after implant-related paresthesia reported greater improvement in deep, superficial, and thermal sensory tests with PBM plus vitamin-B supplementation than with sham plus the same supplement (Gerayeli et al. 2026). An earlier 35-person sham-controlled trial found no significant difference in neurosensory improvement: 46.7% with laser and 38.5% with control (Miloro et al. 2018).

Animal evidence

Ten animal publications are indexed: nine rat studies and one rabbit study. These models provide mechanistic context but do not establish sensory recovery in people.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The post-extraction trial used 808-nm continuous-wave PBM at 100 mW and 9 J/cm² for 90 seconds per site over 15 sessions. The implant-related trial used 810 nm at 200 mW and 6 J/cm² for eight sessions over four weeks. Injury cause, timing, co-interventions, sensory tests, and schedules differ, so these regimens cannot be treated as interchangeable.

Interpretation

The evidence supports a possible improvement in selected sensory outcomes after third-molar extraction or implant-related paresthesia. Certainty is low for these groups and very low for other causes or durable recovery. Small samples, differing injury mechanisms, spontaneous recovery, vitamin-B co-interventions, and one retracted report limit confidence. Larger sham-controlled studies should stratify by cause and severity, measure objective and patient-reported sensation, report co-interventions, and follow participants longer.

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

Two-point discrimination — no significant pooled effect within 48 hours or at 14 days; SMD −0.63 at 30 days and −1.10 at 60 days (Ma et al. 2023).

Post-extraction hypoesthesia — day-30 change −2.6 ± 1.7 mm with direct PBM versus −0.8 ± 1.1 mm with sham; monofilament grade improved in 80% versus 25% (Ma et al. 2026).

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Low for sensory recovery after selected post-extraction or implant-related injury. Very low for other causes and durable recovery.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

The 2023 review pooled small trials, found no significant early two-point-discrimination effect, and included relatively few third-molar extraction injuries. Newer sham-controlled trials are also small and address selected groups; the post-extraction trial gave mecobalamin to every group, while implant-related participants received vitamin-B supplementation. Sensory recovery can occur over time without PBM, and the indexed literature includes one retracted trial report. These limits support low certainty for selected causes and very low certainty beyond them.
